# Geometric rate groups and exact phase-start compensation

This note independently audits the affine rate-slice theorem and proves two refinements. Phase compensation is an exact measure identity, including the exterior surface atom at the transition rate. More substantially, compensation cannot pass between different limiting affine zero hyperplanes: each positive-proportionality group of actual geometric cells has its own positive-rate uniform kernel. An explicit two-plane convex-body example shows that compensation within one group really occurs.

These are statements about actual geometric active cells, never arbitrary contact-row labels. They do not exclude defects at a selected minimum and do not establish the numerical OC bound.

## 1. Independent audit and hypotheses

Read in full:

* `candidate 1ec792c66c5ddc47`, including its finite-cell Section 8;
* `candidate d3b1d852e0e3ae4b`;
* `candidate 91145d6ea212266a`;
* the saved independent audit `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.

The saved audit concerns the full-body rate kernel, rather than the affine-slice extension. The affine-slice proof passes an independent analytic audit. The anchor projection is exact, the factor in coarea is `1/(M_j lambda_j |c_j|)`, and integration on a rate interval strictly after the anchor threshold gives local measure-valued domination. Weak closure of the positive measure-concavity inequality is valid with positive-mass inputs. This closure permits collapsed supports and atoms; it does not assert uniform density on the limit face. In Section 8 a maximal-height anchor need not be interior: convexity alone gives the requisite homothety. Cells of positive limiting constant affine height carry no positive-rate mass. The full positive kernel excludes atoms at their positive thresholds, and bounds the one-sided post-threshold measures. These facts justify the displayed compensation inequality there.

Independently reran the three existing exact checkers: affine rate slices, 3,191 checks PASS; capwise rate flux/incidences, 9,256 checks PASS; full uniform-rate audit, 6,559 checks PASS. These support the algebraic calibrations; the general convergence arguments were read and checked separately.

The full-body and capwise flux proofs also pass with their stated hypotheses. Monomials of positive degree avoid the moving `L_j=1` cutoff. Bulk logarithm uniform integrability removes the bulk derivative term. Radial weights and affine-plane weights must remain present. A capwise positive kernel requires absence of its section defect; a generic nonparallel cap can still fractionally select boundary mass. None of these results permits a freely chosen normal or source label on the other side of a flux identity.

For the nontrivial new results assume `d>=2` and fix one fiber. Let positive convex bodies `K_j` converge to a positive convex body `K`, within a fixed ball. Let

    L_j = min_{1<=i<=k} A_ij > 0 on K_j,
    A_ij(X) = a_ij + c_ij . X -> A_i(X),
    L = min_i A_i > 0 in int K,
    lambda_j -> 0,  M_j -> M > 0.

Assume the inverse masses are bounded, the bulk logarithms are uniformly integrable, the surface positive-log masses are bounded, and the actual rates

    r_j = lambda_j (-log L_j)_+

lie in one compact interval. These are the existing rate-kernel hypotheses. Choose a fixed `o` in `int K`; it is in `int K_j` eventually. Put `b_i=A_i(o)>0`. The geometric cells are

    C_ij = K_j intersect {A_ij <= A_lj for all l}.

Merge identical planes at each index and select a subsequence with fixed merging pattern. Discard cells of zero volume. Full-dimensional cells partition volume up to null sets. Their exterior boundary traces partition the surface of `K_j` almost everywhere. At a tie hyperplane coinciding with a body facet, only the cell on the interior side has an interior trace there. Thus a duplicated boundary contribution is not introduced.

Retain all actual joint limits. Write `zetahat_i` for the inverse defect of cell `i`, with its rate. The finite-cell slice theorem provides a threshold `R_i`, and decreasing conditional measures `gamma_i(r)` for `r>R_i`. They vanish before their threshold, and

    zetahat_i | {r>0} = gamma_i(r) dr.

Here and below a value at the threshold itself is immaterial to this density.

For `d=1` the defect conclusions are trivial under the same inverse-mass hypothesis: Fatou gives integrability of `1/L` on the limiting interval. A finite-PL positive concave function vanishing at an endpoint is bounded above there by a constant times endpoint distance, contradicting that integrability. Hence `L` is positive on the closed interval, and coefficient/Hausdorff convergence gives a uniform positive floor on `K_j`. Both defects vanish. For `d=0`, positivity of the limiting parameter on the point similarly excludes defects.

## 2. Exact global compensation and canonical one-sided versions

Let `B(dX,dR)` be the radially weighted full exterior surface-log defect and let

    V = M sum_i b_i zetahat_i = integral U_R B(dX,dR),

where `U_R` is uniform probability measure on `[0,R]` for `R>0`, and `U_0=delta_0`. Define, for `r>0`,

    F_+(r) = integral_{R>r} B(dX,dR)/R,
    F_-(r) = integral_{R>=r} B(dX,dR)/R.

These are finite physical measures, locally bounded on positive rate intervals. `F_+` is weakly right-continuous, `F_-` gives its left limit, and

    F_-(r) - F_+(r) = B(dX,{r})/r.                 (1)

On every interval avoiding the finitely many thresholds, the decreasing right-continuous versions of the cell densities obey

    M sum_i b_i gamma_i(r) = F_+(r).              (2)

Indeed they agree almost everywhere by the joint density identity; two right-continuous measure-valued functions agreeing almost everywhere agree everywhere, tested first on a countable dense family of continuous functions. Local domination by `F_+` bounds every cell density on either side of any positive threshold. A decreasing cell consequently has finite weak right and left limits there. Passing to both one-sided limits of (2) proves the exact measure equality, for every `R>0`,

    sum_{R_i<R} b_i [gamma_i(R-) - gamma_i(R+)]
      = sum_{R_i=R} b_i gamma_i(R+)
          + B(dX,{R})/(M R).                       (3)

Every term displayed in (3) is a positive measure. Cells with threshold greater than `R` are absent. The equality is at the same physical positions, rather than only at the level of total masses. It applies also when `R` is not a threshold, in which case the first sum accounts for the entire exterior rate atom.

For a distributional formulation, let `D_i=-d gamma_i` be the positive measure-valued Stieltjes derivative on `(R_i,infinity)`, including all post-start jumps. On compact positive-rate intervals it is finite; if `R_i>0`, the finite right limit also gives finiteness down to that endpoint. Then

    sum_i b_i D_i
      = sum_{i:R_i>0} b_i gamma_i(R_i+) delta_{R_i}
          + B(dX,dr)/(M r)                         (4)

on physical-position times positive-rate space. There is no start term at zero in this open interval. Both sides are locally finite, since `1/r` is bounded on compact subsets of `(0,infinity)` and there are finitely many starts. Formula (3) is its atom identity. No finiteness as `r` decreases to zero is claimed without the indicated weighting.

## 3. Interfaces between distinct affine groups have no positive-rate defect

Place two limiting affine functions in the same group exactly when

    A_i = alpha A_k as affine functions, for some alpha>0.

For planes whose zero sets meet `K`, this is equivalent to equality of their zero hyperplanes: their positive values at `o` fix the positive orientation. Positive constant planes, and any plane bounded away from zero on `K`, have no positive-rate contribution.

Consider an actual interface between cells `i` and `k` in different groups. It is contained in the hyperplane

    P_ik,j = {A_ij=A_kj},

and its parameter there is `A_ij=A_kj`. If the limiting gradients `c_i,c_k` are not parallel, the norm of the tangential gradient of `A_ij` on `P_ik,j` is

    |c_ij wedge c_kj| / |c_ij-c_kj|,

which has a positive lower bound. All interfaces remain in a common ball. Coarea on their containing hyperplanes therefore gives, uniformly for small `epsilon>0`,

    integral_{interface, 0<A_ij<epsilon} (-log A_ij)_+ dH_{d-1}
        <= C integral_0^epsilon (-log s) ds.          (5)

For `d=2`, the transverse measure in this coarea estimate is counting measure, bounded by the single hyperplane section; the same estimate holds. For `d>2`, the transverse sections are in a common ball. Replacing the actual interface by the whole bounded hyperplane slice only increases the integral.

If the limiting gradients are parallel, different groups cannot have a common zero point in `K`. Otherwise the two zero hyperplanes coincide and positivity at `o` puts them in the same group. Compactness thus bounds the common interface value away from zero for all sufficiently large `j`. A limiting positive constant plane gives the same conclusion. These alternatives prove uniform integrability of the interface logarithms in every intergroup case.

In particular, for every integer `m>=1`,

    integral_{intergroup interface} (-log L_j)_+ r_j^m dH_{d-1} -> 0.    (6)

To see this directly, use (5) for a uniformly small logarithmic tail. On its complement the logarithm is bounded and `r_j` tends uniformly to zero. The compact rate bound controls the tail. There are finitely many cell pairs.

## 4. A separate positive-rate uniform kernel for each geometric group

Fix a group `G`. Let `chi_Gj` be the exterior boundary trace of the union of its full-dimensional cells. Extract the actual joint measure limit of

    chi_Gj (-log L_j)_+ eta_j delta_{r_j}.

Let `bhat_G` denote its restriction to positive rates. These measures are positive, and their sum is the positive-rate restriction of the full exterior defect. No labelwise split is invented: the selectors are the actual active geometric groups.

For `m>=1`, apply Gauss--Green to

    phi (-log L_j)_+ r_j^m

on each cell of `G` and sum. Internal interfaces of the group cancel exactly: the function is continuous, and the two normals are opposite. The remaining interfaces are between different groups, whose contributions tend to zero by (6). The bulk test-gradient term tends to zero by bulk-log uniform integrability. The a.e. derivative on cell `i` is exactly

    -(m+1) r_j^m c_ij / A_ij.

The actual joint inverse measures therefore give

    - integral phi n r^m d bhat_G
        = M (m+1) sum_{i in G} c_i integral phi r^m d zetahat_i.      (7)

Only positive rates matter in (7); possible rate-zero interface effects are neither identified nor discarded in an unweighted identity. The use of `m>=1` makes them invisible legitimately.

On the limiting exterior normal bundle put `h(n,X)=n.(X-o)>0`. On the inverse defect of cell `i`, `A_i(X)=0`, so `c_i.(X-o)=-b_i`. Dot (7) with `X-o`, keeping an arbitrary continuous physical test. With

    B_G = projection_(X,r) [h bhat_G],
    V_G = M sum_{i in G} b_i zetahat_i | {r>0},

we get, for every `m>=1`,

    integral phi r^m dV_G = (m+1)^(-1) integral phi r^m dB_G.        (8)

Both measures are positive and finite, and neither has an atom at rate zero. Applying the uniform kernel to `B_G` has the moments on the right. Polynomials with zero constant term determine a finite measure on every compact interval away from zero; uniform approximation of continuous functions vanishing near zero and then monotone exhaustion identifies the measures on all positive rates. Hence

    V_G(dX,ds) = integral_{R>0} U_R(ds) B_G(dX,dR).                 (9)

In particular the group density

    F_G(r) = M sum_{i in G} b_i gamma_i(r)

has a decreasing right-continuous version. The proof of Section 2 now gives (3) and (4) separately within each group, with `B_G` in place of `B` and with all sums restricted to `G`.

This is the new invariant: a positive delayed start can be paid only by a loss in the same limiting affine zero-hyperplane group, together with that group's exterior rate atom. An arbitrary source partition of a cell has no such conclusion. Nor does (9) identify the group's external normal with its common gradient.

As one immediate consequence, if the limiting affine zero hyperplanes are pairwise distinct, each relevant group has one cell. A cell with `R_i>0` cannot start nontrivially: the left side of (3) within its singleton group is zero at `R_i`, forcing `gamma_i(R_i+)=0`. Monotonicity then forces `gamma_i(r)=0` for all `r>R_i`. Thus every positive-rate contributing cell in that case has threshold zero.

## 5. An exact actual compensated start within one group

Fix `k>1` and `0<R_1<R_2`. Put

    lambda_j = 1/j,  a_j = 1/j,
    eta_lj = exp(-R_l j),  u=t-a_j,  t=x+y,
    K_j = {x,y>=0, a_j<=x+y<=1},
    L_j = c_j min(u+eta_1j, k u+eta_2j).

Choose `c_j` so that the mean of `log L_j` on `K_j` is zero. The two affine planes converge to `c t` and `c k t`, where `c=exp(1/2)`. Indeed the second branch occurs only for

    0<=u<=u_j^*=(eta_1j-eta_2j)/(k-1),

an exponentially short collar, and its logarithmic integral tends to zero; off it the usual truncated-triangle mean-log limit is `-1/2`.

Use `M_j=|K_j| -> M=1/2`. The inverse masses are bounded. This follows directly from `dX=t dt dv`, `0<=v<=1`, and the two rational integrals:

    integral_{u_j^*}^{1-a_j} (a_j+u)/(u+eta_1j) du -> 1+R_1,
    integral_0^{u_j^*} (a_j+u)/(k u+eta_2j) du -> (R_2-R_1)/k.

The first cell has threshold zero and the second threshold `R_1`. Coarea with the actual rate gives their positive-rate conditional inverse measures, both physically at the limiting vertex:

    gamma_1(r) = (2/c) delta_0,       0<r<R_1;
    gamma_2(r) = (2/(c k)) delta_0,   R_1<r<R_2;

and zero elsewhere. For example, on branch 2, `dL=c_j k dt`, while `t/lambda_j ->1` on a compact subinterval of `(R_1,R_2)`, giving `1/(M c k)=2/(c k)`. The analogous first-branch calculation gives `2/c`.

For an interior anchor `o`, write `t_o=o_x+o_y`. Then

    b_1=c t_o,   b_2=c k t_o.

The weighted loss of cell 1 at `R_1` and the weighted birth of cell 2 are both `2 t_o delta_0`. The actual exterior surface-log defect is only on the bottom edge, with normal `n_0=-(1,1)/sqrt(2)`:

    bhat = sqrt(2) R_2 delta_(n_0,0,R_2),
    B = t_o R_2 delta_(0,R_2).

All other exterior edges have uniformly integrable logarithms. There is no exterior atom at `R_1`, so the compensation at that rate is exact and nonzero. The group density is `t_o delta_0` throughout `(0,R_2)`, exactly as (9) requires.

The artificial interface `t=a_j+u_j^*` has a log defect `sqrt(2)R_1` at rate `R_1`. Its outward normal for cell 1 is `n_0`, and for cell 2 it is `-n_0`. The two radial interface measures are therefore `+t_o R_1 delta_(0,R_1)` and its negative. Their uniform kernels create precisely the interval laws `(0,R_1)` and `(R_1,R_2)`, and cancel when the geometric group is summed.

This example uses actual convex bodies and a genuine concave two-plane parameter, satisfying the compactness hypotheses above. It is not asserted to be a selected deepest stationary configuration, and its collapsing cell does not supply a uniformly interior source mark. It certifies that actual convex interface geometry alone cannot forbid same-group compensated starts.

## 6. The group kernel does not imply groupwise slice concavity

The existing convex-profile example gives an exact limitation, without requiring a new numerical search. In dimension three, with `s in [0,1]`, take

    H(s)=max(2-s,1+s),
    A(s)=max(2-s,17/10,1+s),
    E={A=H}=[0,3/10] union [7/10,1],
    delta_j=1/j, eta_j=exp(-j), lambda_j=rho/j,
    K_j={s in [0,1], x,y>=0, delta_j A(s)<=t=x+y<=1},
    L_j=c_j[t-delta_j H(s)+eta_j], c_j->c=exp(1/2).

Both limiting affine planes are `c t`, so they form one group. At a fixed rate `0<r<rho`, the admissibility condition of the level surface is

    delta_j[A(s)-H(s)] <= exp(-rj/rho)/c_j-eta_j.

Its limiting tangential support is precisely `E`. On either active piece, coarea in `(s,t,v)`, where `x=vt`, has Jacobian `t`; `t/lambda_j -> H(s)/rho`. With `M=1/2`, the group's conditional inverse density is therefore

    gamma_G(r,ds) = [2 H(s)/(c rho)] 1_E(s) ds,
                 0<r<rho,                          (10)

at physical points `(s,0,0)`. It is zero for `r>rho`. The support is disconnected. Each cell separately has a concave conditional measure on its own interval; their group does not. The group's radial surface law, for an anchor with continuous height `t_o`, is

    B_G = t_o H(s) 1_E(s) ds delta_rho,

and its uniform kernel agrees exactly with `M c t_o gamma_G(r) dr`. Thus (9) is consistent with the failure of groupwise log-concavity.

Every whole-fiber affine majorant still has its own nested convex slices. Those whole-fiber measures are different from the active-cell union and cannot be substituted for it without a separately proved comparison. This example has the actual contact-row realization already documented in `candidate 9a1deed5372bf5ee`; no selected deepest physical stationarity is claimed here.

All group assertions above are fiberwise. In a finite mixed-integer family the proportionality grouping may differ from one integer base to another. Fiberwise Gauss--Green permits this grouping; it does not create a new globally affine parameter or a new admissible physical variation.

## 7. Exterior normal rigidity for positive-rate geometric defects

There is a further geometric fact, stronger than the averaged vector flux. For every group `G` with nonzero positive-rate exterior defect, choose a representative limiting continuous gradient `c_G`. Then

    bhat_G is supported on n = -c_G/|c_G|.           (11)

This statement concerns the actual active geometric groups. It does not assign exterior normals to arbitrary source-row allocations.

Here is a direct proof. First consider a single affine majorant `A_ij>=L_j>0` on the whole body, with nonzero limiting gradient `c_i`. For its restriction to the rectifiable boundary of `K_j`, the tangential gradient has norm

    |grad_boundary A_ij| = |c_ij-(c_ij.n)n|.

Fix `epsilon_0>0` and restrict to boundary points where this norm is at least `epsilon_0`. Boundary coarea gives

    integral_{A_ij<epsilon, |grad_boundary A_ij|>=epsilon_0}
                     (-log A_ij)_+ dH_{d-1}
       <= (C/epsilon_0) integral_0^epsilon (-log s) ds.             (12)

The uniform constant follows because, for almost every level strictly between the minimum and maximum of `A_ij`, the boundary level set is the relative boundary of the convex section `K_j intersect {A_ij=s}`. Its `(d-2)`-dimensional measure is uniformly bounded in a fixed ball. One elementary bound for an `m`-dimensional convex body's perimeter in a ball of radius `T` is `2m sqrt(m) (2T)^(m-1)`: partition its boundary by a coordinate in which the normal has magnitude at least `1/sqrt(m)` and its sign, then use the injective projection of the corresponding upper or lower convex graph. For `m=1`, this is simply the two endpoints. Thus this use of coarea needs no smoothness or curvature bound.

If the limiting gradient vanishes, `A_i` is a positive constant and has no positive-rate contribution. Otherwise, (12) implies that the positive-rate surface-log measure of `A_ij` can only have limiting normals parallel to `c_i`. Indeed on rates at least `r_0>0`, its value is at most `exp(-r_0/lambda_j)`, and the right side of (12) tends to zero.

The positive parallel normal is impossible. A fixed ball about `o` is contained in `K_j`, so every exterior normal satisfies `n.(X-o)>=r_b>0`. At a limiting point with `A_i(X)=0`, however,

    (c_i/|c_i|).(X-o) = -b_i/|c_i| < 0.

Thus the only possible parallel normal is `-c_i/|c_i|`. On the exterior trace of an active cell `i`, its logarithm is exactly the logarithm of this affine majorant. Restriction can only reduce (12). Since a group has finitely many planes and all their limiting gradients are positive multiples, (11) follows.

In particular the radial support weight is constant on each group's positive-rate defect:

    h(n,X) = h_G := b_i/|c_i|,  i in G.

Writing `mu_G` for the projection of `bhat_G` that forgets its now determined normal, (9) becomes the simpler exact positive-rate identity

    M sum_{i in G} |c_i| zetahat_i | {r>0}
         = integral_{R>0} U_R(ds) mu_G(dX,dR).       (13)

No arbitrary normal/source identification has occurred: the proof first fixes actual whole-fiber affine majorants and their geometric active traces. Likewise (13) does not identify individual cells inside one group, because their artificial interfaces can still exchange rate mass as in Section 5.

## 8. Tail testing also retains the group's rate-zero defect

The same group identity extends to the full defect, including rate zero. This requires the ordinary boundary logarithm to be integrable, as supplied in the existing surface-defect framework. Here is a tail proof which avoids presuming convergence of ordinary group interface allocations.

Use the same actual exterior selectors `chi_Gj`. Their joint logarithmic measures have bounded mass and are bounded above by the full surface-log measures. Off `{L=0}` their limiting part is an ordinary selected logarithmic boundary measure at rate zero, with selector between zero and one. Define `bhat_G^all` to be the restriction of this joint limit to `{L=0}`, retaining every rate, including zero. Define `zetahat_i^all` analogously from the actual cell inverse measures. These are positive finite measures; they sum over groups to the existing full defects. Every one is obtained from actual selectors.

For fixed `T>0` set

    F_j,T = [(-log L_j)_+ - T]_+.

On an active cell its a.e. gradient is

    -1_{L_j<exp(-T)} c_ij/L_j.

Sum its Gauss--Green formula over the cells in `G`, with a bounded `C1` physical test `phi`. Internal interfaces cancel exactly. The norm of the remaining intergroup interface contribution is at most a constant times their logarithmic tails. By (5) and its positive-floor alternative, this upper bound tends to zero uniformly in sufficiently large `j` as `T` tends to infinity. The bulk term involving `F_j,T grad phi` tends uniformly to zero by bulk-log uniform integrability.

The boundary limit for fixed `T` is particularly direct. Write `F_j,T=q_T(L_j)(-log L_j)_+`, where

    q_T(s) = [1-T/(-log s)]_+ for 0<s<1,
    q_T(s)=1 for s<=0, and q_T(s)=0 for s>=1.

This is continuous on the common bounded ambient range of the affine minima. The extension to negative arguments matters only when comparing with the limiting affine minimum at prelimit boundary points outside `K`; it does not change any prelimit integral. Uniform convergence of `L_j` therefore allows passage against the actual joint boundary measures. Its value on the whole defect is exactly one; its ordinary contribution is bounded by the ordinary logarithmic boundary tail, which tends to zero as `T` increases.

For the volume term choose a sequence `T` increasing to infinity for which the limiting inverse measures assign zero mass to `{L=exp(-T)}`. Only countably many levels can be excluded. Uniform convergence of `L_j` and joint weak convergence of the cell inverse measures then pass the low-level indicators. Each limit is its full zero-set defect plus the ordinary inverse measure below that positive level. The latter tends to zero as `T` increases, by integrability of the ordinary inverse measure. Consequently, first letting `j` tend to infinity and then this sequence `T` tend to infinity gives

    - integral phi n d bhat_G^all
        = M sum_{i in G} c_i integral phi d zetahat_i^all.         (14)

The normal-rigidity proof also applies to these full zero-set defects. Away from normals parallel to `c_i`, (12) uniformly controls the logarithmic mass in arbitrarily small `A_ij` collars; hence their weak residual over `A_i=0` is zero, even if its rate is zero. The fixed inball again excludes the positive normal. Thus `bhat_G^all` is supported on `n=-c_G/|c_G|`, and its radial weight is the same constant `h_G`.

Combining (14) with the positive-degree moment identities of Section 4 supplies every moment, including degree zero. Compact rate moment uniqueness now gives the full identity

    M sum_{i in G} |c_i| zetahat_i^all(dX,ds)
        = integral_{R>=0} U_R(ds) mu_G^all(dX,dR),                 (15)

where `mu_G^all` is the projection of `bhat_G^all` forgetting its determined normal and `U_0=delta_0`. In particular

    M sum_{i in G} |c_i| zetahat_i^all(dX,{0})
        = mu_G^all(dX,{0}).                                     (16)

The tail argument establishes exactly the missing zeroth-moment flux; it does not erase a rate-zero defect. The separate source rows of the contact construction still need not coincide with these geometric cells or groups.
